item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] The agonising wait for Gaza’s missing
item.description:
The agonising wait for Gaza’s missing

Three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, Palestinian families are still searching for answers about thousands of relatives who vanished during the war.

Some disappeared during Israeli ground attacks on their neighbourhoods or displacement camps. Others went missing while searching for aid, checking on their homes or travelling near the so-called Yellow Line.

For their families, the absence of any definitive answer has left them suspended between hope and grief, unsure whether to keep waiting or begin mourning.

According to the Independent Commission for Human Rights, more than 11,000 people in Gaza remain unaccounted for, including those believed to be buried beneath the rubble and those suspected of enforced disappearance.

The Palestinian Centre for Missing and Forcibly Disappeared estimates that between 2,500 and 3,000 people are suspected of enforced disappearance, having gone missing or lost contact with their families since the start of the war and through the ceasefire announced on 9 October 2025.

Their fate remains unknown, with Israeli authorities still withholding the names of all those detained from the Strip and failing to identify approximately 620 bodies returned to Gaza.

Middle East Eye spoke to three families whose relatives disappeared during the war about their hopes, fears and the long wait for answers.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Queuing for water and phone charging: What survival looks like in Gaza
item.description:
Queuing for water and phone charging: What survival looks like in Gaza

Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Tue, 10/06/2026 - 13:15
As Israel's genocide enters its fourth year, daily life for Palestinians has been reduced to finding food and water while coping with loss and displacement

Nearly two years after Raja al-Shawish's husband went missing at an Israeli checkpoint, she says she no longer feels like a woman.

Since his disappearance, she has had to bear the responsibility of raising her children alone, from the moment she wakes up, until the time she goes to sleep.

The routines that once gave her a sense of herself have been replaced by the daily demands of survival, leaving little room for the life she once knew or the woman she once was.

"My husband was with me during the first year of the genocide, and although it was harsh, he would carry the burden with me and make it feel less devastating," Raja told Middle East Eye from an Unrwa classroom in western Gaza City that has been her home for around two years.

"Since he disappeared, and during the starvation, I have sold all my gold - except for one piece - to feed our children. I kept the last piece for when he returns. I will sell it then and use the money to celebrate."

Raja's husband, Muhamed, 48, went missing on 21 October 2024 after Israeli forces invaded their neighbourhood in northern Gaza and forced them south.

According to an eyewitness, Israeli forces ordered Muhamed to walk as a human shield. 

When he refused, the soldiers violently beat him. The eyewitness said they had no further information about his fate since.

"I contacted the Red Cross and HaMoked [an Israel-based human rights organisation], but they told me that the Israeli authorities do not acknowledge that he is being held by them," Raja said.

"He has been gone for two years, but I live with the certainty that he is still alive. People often come to me and tell me, 'You have to consider that he may have been killed'. I tell them no.

"I can't even imagine that he was killed. Deep inside, I am certain that he is just being detained."

Since Israel launched its genocidal war on 7 October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including more than 21,500 children - of which 1,029 are under the age of one.

The scale of the killings remains difficult to establish as more than 11,200 Palestinians have either been reported missing or are unaccounted for.

The killing has also continued despite a ceasefire being signed on 10 October 2025.

'It's not just about the destruction, the losses and the people who are gone. More importantly, it's about the social habits that have disappeared and how society itself has changed'

- Raja al-Shawish, mother

Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded another 4,131, including journalists, doctors, first responders, writers, artists and footballers, among others.

The devastation has drawn widespread international condemnation and prompted legal proceedings against Israel over its conduct in the enclave and its occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

At the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Israel faces a case brought by South Africa alleging violations of the Genocide Convention, in which the court has found that Palestinians in Gaza have a plausible right to be protected from acts of genocide. 

Separate proceedings have also addressed the legality of Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.

At the International Criminal Court (ICC), prosecutors have issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, over alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The Israeli government has repeatedly rejected such allegations and defended its attacks on residential buildings, schools, hospitals and other civilian sites by saying that Hamas or other Palestinian armed groups operate from them.

'My life has disappeared'

For Raja, however, the disappearance of her husband has meant losing more than the person she shared her life with.

The weight of carrying responsibilities she once shared with him, while attempting to survive an ongoing genocide, has gradually erased the woman she once was.

"My life has disappeared. I stopped seeing myself as a woman. I wasn't like this before. When people saw me before the genocide, they would ask, 'Are you a professional?’ because I was always so put-together and dressed nicely," Raja continued.

"Now people ask me: 'Why have you let yourself go like this? Are you in mourning?'

"I tell them: 'No, I'm not in mourning. My husband isn't here. My love isn't here. Who am I supposed to dress up for?"

For two years, she says she has put her life, and that of her children, on hold.

Over the past couple of months, she turned down multiple marriage proposals for one of her daughters, insisting that the girl could not get married without her father there.

Eventually, after people urged her to reconsider, she agreed. Her daughter's wedding is planned for the end of October, and Shawish is holding on to the hope that her husband will return before then.

But the changes to her family's life are only part of a broader transformation she has witnessed around her.

"Life has changed completely. And it's not just about the destruction, the losses and the people who are gone. More importantly, it's about the social habits that have disappeared and how society itself has changed. Everyone has become irritable, and there are conflicts between people," she added.

"All of this is because of the poverty, displacement, overcrowding and difficult living conditions we have endured. This is something that might be impossible to fix."

Survival as a full-time job

But for most Palestinians, the day starts with more immediate questions: where to find water, what to eat and how to get through the next few hours.

At dawn, Nihad al-Skafi joins the queues for water.

The 36-year-old father of five spends his mornings securing what his family needs to get through the day.

"From the moment we wake up until we go to sleep, all that occupies us are basic survival tasks: collecting water, finding food, eating, staying alive, then sleeping,” Skafi told MEE as he filled a water container from a hose emerging from the ground in a displacement camp in western Gaza.

"The water I'm collecting now is only for washing and bathing, and it is extremely salty. For drinking water, we have to wait for the water truck to arrive every other day. We wake up at dawn to take our place in the long queue."

Before the genocide, Skafi, originally a resident of Shujaiya, worked as a construction worker. Today, he waits his turn to receive food parcels from charities and relief organisations to feed his family.

By midday, the question becomes what there is to eat.

"If we get food, then we have something to eat for lunch. But if we can't get a hot meal, we have to figure out what we’re going to eat and how we're going to get it. Then comes the struggle to find firewood and get a fire going just to cook. Every step is a struggle," he continued.

"Our gas cylinder ran out, and now we have to wait around 40 days until it's our turn to refill it. Until then, we have no choice but to go back to using firewood."

Cooking gas remains severely scarce in Gaza despite an agreement allowing fuel and cooking gas to enter under the October 2025 ceasefire.

As a result, supplies have remained far below demand, leaving families waiting weeks or months for their turn.

The Gaza General Petroleum Authority publishes beneficiary lists as new shipments arrive and distributes the available gas according to those lists.

Making money from scarcity

By afternoon, another basic task comes into focus: finding electricity to charge mobile phones.

With Gaza's electricity infrastructure almost entirely destroyed during the genocide, most Palestinians have no access to a regular power supply.

The agonising wait for Gaza’s missing
Read More »

Many rely on private generators or solar panels for electricity, while those without them have to pay to charge their phones at small charging points.

Electricity from private generators now costs around 30 to 35 shekels ($10-$11) per kilowatt-hour.

For Hilal al-Zuwaidi, 34, this has become a source of income, a job he never imagined doing.

Before the war, he worked in construction and traded fruit. Today, he earns a small income charging mobile phones for displaced people and residents.

"This is a new kind of job that we didn't know before the war," he said.

"Displaced people and those living nearby bring their phones every day to charge them. I charge one phone for one shekel if they bring their own charger, and two shekels if they don't."

Zuweidi lamented however that repeated power cuts often shut down his generator and he "struggles with the cost of electricity".

"Today, a family of four with phones needs to spend around 120 shekels a month just to charge their phones. Not everyone can afford that when most people have lost their jobs and have no source of income at all," he said.

"So many people come to charge their phones on credit. I have an entire notebook recording what people owe me. Some families have accumulated debts of 300 or 400 shekels."

Before the war, the 34-year-old earned around 400 to 500 shekels ($131-$164) a week. Today, he earns roughly the same amount over an entire month.

"We're just trying to make a living out of whatever we can. We never had charging points like this in Gaza before," he said.

"It's just another thing we never imagined we'd have to deal with because of the war."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Naza: Why the world watches only when Israelis document genocide
item.description:
Naza: Why the world watches only when Israelis document genocide

Submitted by Dr Omar Abdel-Mannan on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 07:30
A film built on Israeli soldiers' accounts wins acclaim, while the Palestinian doctors and journalists who documented the genocide in Gaza for three years struggle for recognition
Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, with the New York Film Festival's artistic director Dennis Lim, speak onstage at the premiere of Naza, 26 September 2026 (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images via AFP)
On

Would anyone be calling Naza a masterpiece if a Palestinian had made it?

The filmmaker Daniele Rugo and I were asking each other that as we walked out of a screening at the Zurich Film Festival of the new documentary in which 24 anonymous Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers describe how they killed Palestinians in Gaza. Daniele's own film, Life Support, which my organisation, Health Workers 4 Palestine, is proud to have backed as associate producers, was having its international premiere.

Between us, we had watched Palestinian doctors, nurses and journalists document the destruction of Gaza in real time for three years, many of them at the cost of their lives. Neither of us could remember their work being received like this.

Since its premiere in Venice, where it won the Special Jury Prize, Naza has been greeted as a reckoning. Critics have called it essential, devastating, the new authority on what Israel has done in Gaza. Its directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, made the Oscar-winning No Other Land with their Palestinian colleagues Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal.

Their new film, produced by the Guardian with Jonathan Glazer as executive producer, sits its witnesses on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, faces hidden, and lets them explain, calmly and in detail, how the killing was done.

It is an important document, and it took courage to make, but our question would not go away. Had a Palestinian filmmaker brought us the same truth from the other end of the rifle, would it have premiered in Venice, been co-produced by a national newspaper and been talked about for the Oscars? We both suspected we knew the answer.

No confession needed

The title, Naza, is a Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage: the civilians Israel decides in advance it is willing to kill. The rules of engagement described in the film allowed for up to 20 of them per target. That number alone should end any remaining debate about intent.

What stayed with me, though, was less a statistic than the tone. These men and women are billed as whistleblowers, but whistleblowing implies conscience. What I heard instead was procedure: targets sketched on notepads, strikes recounted like shift handovers, homes full of families reduced to a ratio. Some had doubts about strategy, or about whether any of it worked, but remorse for the people they killed was almost entirely absent.

We never needed them to confess, because the genocide has been on camera, in full, from the beginning, filmed by the people living through it and by those who went in to treat them

Their faces are hidden and their names will never be known. Palestinians and their supporters who have criticised the film for shielding self-confessed war criminals are right to ask what accountability looks like when perpetrators are granted both anonymity and a festival premiere.

Doctors are trained to listen for what patients leave out. What these soldiers leave out is "sorry".

We never needed them to confess, because the genocide has been recorded on camera, in full, from the beginning, filmed by the people living through it and by those who went in to treat them.

Gaza: Doctors Under Attack, directed by Karim Shah, documented the systematic destruction of Gaza's health system: hospitals besieged, medics detained, colleagues killed. The BBC commissioned it and then refused to broadcast it, and it took Channel 4 to finally show it, in July 2025.

Daniele's film, Life Support, follows international doctors who entered Gaza between October 2023 and September 2025. It is built from footage they shot on their phones in overwhelmed wards and from the work of two Palestinian cinematographers from Gaza, Mahmoud Abou Hamda and Suleiman Hejjy. You see children treated on hospital floors, and formula, pain relief and surgical instruments held at the border. More than 1,700 health workers have been killed. Nothing on screen needs explaining.

Yes, most of the doctors speaking are white and British, but they know exactly why they are on screen. They centre their Palestinian colleagues throughout, the ones working marathon shifts while grieving their own families, and describe themselves as a vessel for those colleagues to be heard.

That is the film's Trojan horse: a familiar face from an NHS hospital brings in audiences who would never otherwise sit through a film about Gaza, and then hands the story back to the Palestinians it belongs to.

Rather than asking you to infer genocide from the testimony of those who carried it out, these films show you its consequences on the bodies of children.

Believing Palestinians

Why does Naza get the red carpet when Palestinian testimony so rarely does? Part of the answer is uncomfortable, and we should say it plainly.

Western audiences have been trained to treat Palestinian testimony as suspect, and for three years Palestinian doctors and journalists were dismissed as propagandists. The death toll, now more than 74,000, was footnoted as "according to the Hamas-run health ministry" until it could no longer be denied. Palestinian journalists have been killed in record numbers telling this story, and still their reporting was treated as a claim rather than a fact.

When an Israeli filmmaker presents the same reality through the mouths of Israeli soldiers, it suddenly becomes credible, essential, Oscar-worthy. That is not the fault of Abraham and Szor, who have consistently used their platform to amplify Palestinian voices. Szor herself has acknowledged that "Palestinian journalists have been reporting this for the last years".

It is the fault of an industry and a press that will only believe Palestinians once an Israeli vouches for them, and no appeal to balance or to standards of evidence changes what that is: anti-Palestinian racism.

Look at how other films have fared. Built from footage his own medical team shot on their phones, The Mission follows the British-Iraqi surgeon Mohammad Tahir through Gaza's collapsing operating theatres. It is every bit as devastating as Naza and shows the genocide through the eyes of an Arab doctor, yet it was reportedly turned down by every major film festival.

Gaza: Doctors Under Attack was shelved by our national broadcaster and only reached audiences through Channel 4, before going on to win a Bafta. Meanwhile, a film centring the perpetrators was co-produced by a national newspaper and celebrated in its pages.

I am not asking anyone to boycott Naza. Watch it, and let it strip away the last excuse anyone has for saying they did not know, but do not mistake it for the definitive account. That belongs to the people of Gaza, and to the doctors, nurses and paramedics, Palestinian above all, who stayed and kept working while their hospitals were bombed around them.

If you watch one film about Gaza this autumn, make it three. Watch Naza to understand how the killing was organised, then Life Support and Doctors Under Attack to see who it was done to. Ask yourself afterwards which you were more ready to believe, and why.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Jewish, 94, and arrested for supporting Palestine Action: Margaret Owen on Ed Miliband and the right to protest
item.description:
Jewish, 94, and arrested for supporting Palestine Action: Margaret Owen on Ed Miliband and the right to protest

Submitted by Katherine Hearst on Tue, 10/06/2026 - 12:26
Owen OBE, a friend of Miliband's late mother, was arrested at a vigil calling on Burnham's government to lift the ban on Palestine Action outside the party conference
Owen being arrested outside the Labour Party conference, 27 September 2026, Liverpool (Amelia Halls)
Off

At 94-years-old, former human rights lawyer Margaret Owen had been trying for months to get arrested.

Jewish and an old friend of the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's mother, she said she had persistently sat, along with hundreds of other pensioners, at silent vigils holding paper signs which read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”

But while others were hauled away by the police, she said she had “failed miserably”.

“I’ve been holding that sign a long time,” Owen told Middle East Eye. She even mounted it in her front room window, and sent photographs to the Metropolitan police, to no avail.

“Even if it’s behind glass, they should have arrested me,” she said. 

But on 27 September, at a protest outside the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, she was finally granted her wish.

“I was quite proud to join the arrestees last Sunday,” she said.

Owen recalled that she was among around 200 other people, “many of us old, disabled. There were a lot of white hairs around, people with crutches, somebody was in a wheelchair.

“We were just sitting quietly with our placards round our necks, and then we see the police wandering through the crowd and photographing at random with their cameras, and then they begin to encircle people,” she told MEE.

Owen has a bad back and struggled to climb into the back of the police van, so she sat up front with a police officer.

“She looked really cruel and vicious when she was arresting me. But when I sat next to her in the van, I looked her in the face and said, “I’m so sorry for you. This is not what you joined the police force for.”

Owen said the officer's face “completely crumbled, she suddenly became human again”.

She said was driven “a long way away” to a police station where she was finger printed and issued her bail conditions which stipulate she must report to a police station on 27 December.

“I think they’re trying to ruin our Christmas,” she said, smiling.

“We are actually now descending and embracing all the features of a police state. It's very, very worrying indeed.”

Defend our Juries (DoJ), the campaign group that called the protest, reported that after over 16 hours, 150 arrests were made.

Merseyside Police told MEE that it does not comment on individual cases, but confirmed that " 83 people were arrested on suspicion of wearing or displaying an item, or publishing an image, in support of a proscribed organisation, and a further 105 people were reported for summons".

"As with all significant policing operations, a debrief process will take place to identify any learning and inform future operational planning," it added.

Starmer’s government proscribed Palestine Action in July 2025, making expressions of support for, or membership of the group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Since then, DoJ estimates that some 3,850 people have been arrested, with at least 2,250 charges for allegedly expressing support for the banned group.

The group’s co-founder, Huda Ammori, is appealing a Court of Appeal decision earlier this year upholding the proscription as lawful.

The case is due to be heard at the Supreme Court later this year.

A Home Office spokesperson told MEE that the proscription "followed a rigorous and evidence-based decision-making process, endorsed by Parliament".

They added that the Court of Appeal, which overturned a High Court ruling finding the ban to be unlawful, found that the group "carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence".

“The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right,” they said.

Match words with actions

As Owen was being hauled away, Miliband addressed the conference, declaring a “reset” in Labour’s approach to foreign policy. 

He condemned “ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank”, Israel’s “war crimes in Gaza”, and its “illegal occupation of Palestine”, vowing to “match words with actions”.

Addressing the "millions of people... who were moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people," he said: "We hear you, you were right.”

“That gave us huge cause for hope,” Owen said, but warned that the raft of sanctions against Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary “wasn't enough for us". 

"He didn't, and he couldn't go far enough, because he has to deal with a very fractured Labour party," she added.

Activists have pointed to the glaring discrepancy between Miliband’s words and the now-familiar sight of white-haired protesters being arrested for supporting Palestine Action.

Burnham’s government, and Miliband in particular, is facing mounting pressure to reverse the controversial ban.

Footage circulated online showed Miliband being accosted by activists in a Pizza Express minutes away from where protesters were being carted away for holding the signs.

Miliband ‘looking at’ whether Palestine Action ban was sensible, argues mass arrests 'unintended'
Read More »

In the recording, an activist is heard informing the foreign secretary that “200 people, 100 metres from here are being arrested” and inviting him to “have a conversation” with them.

“They’re being arrested for holding pieces of paper, Ed,” he said.

Miliband responds that he is “happy to have them chat to me”, but that he was currently speaking to his constituents.

Subsequently, Miliband said in an interview with LBC: “I believe in the right to protest”, but said he would let the ban's Supreme Court appeal hearing “play out”.

Responding to a question from Andrew Marr about the arrests of "grannies and vicars", Miliband said he didn’t think it was “anyone’s intent” to "criminalise" them as a result of the proscription.

On Tuesday, DoJ wrote to Miliband on behalf of Owen and another arrestee, 76-year-old Jonathan Porritt CBE, accepting his offer of a meeting discuss the proscription. 

Responding to Miliband's comments about the arrests, the letter says that the elderly arrestees "have not just been criminalised. They are being prosecuted by your government as terrorists, under the most draconian branch of the criminal law".

“That's an important concession that the government has made. This is not the intention. This is not working as it should be working,” former government lawyer and DoJ co-founder Tim Crosland told MEE.

He said that the acknowledgement is “really significant” to the appeal hearing at the Supreme Court which will assess the ban’s proportionality.

“When the government itself is saying this is a disproportionate interference, it's a bit difficult to see how they defend the case now.”

Crosland noted that Miliband's deferral to the courts “feels disingenuous”, noting that the Home Office is defending the appeal against a High Court ruling that the proscription should be quashed.

“The government's got a choice. At any moment it could concede the appeal,” Crosland said.

Burnham has been less explicit in critiquing the ban.

When asked by Nick Ferrari whether he considered the sign holding vigils to be “terrorist activity” he conceded that the elderly arrestees sit at one end of the Palestine Action “spectrum”, with activists who have “carried out attacks" on military sites on the “extreme end”.

‘She would have ticked Ed off’

Owen can claim a connection with Miliband. She was a close friend of his mother, Marion Kozak, a Polish Holocaust survivor and feminist-socialist campaigner who was a member of Jews for Justice for Palestinians.

Kozak, who died in May, witnessed the Nazi occupation of her hometown Czestochowa.

“She’s one of the women I really admire so much,” Owen said.

Palestine Action: Police arrest protesters throughout the night outside Labour conference
Read More »

Owen said that she, Kozak and Marlene Hobsbawm - the wife of Marxist historian Eric Hobsbawm - were known as the “three M’s”.

“She was incredibly modest, but incredibly strong in her calls for justice and for supporting victims of injustice,” she said, adding that Kozak “had always been for the Palestinian people”.

Reflecting on what Kozak would have made of Miliband’s policy shift on Israel, Owen said: "I think she would have ticked Ed off."

“And yet I salute him, because I think he's made a dramatic shift in our foreign policy," Owen said.

"That is a chink of light in the dark tunnel. We must encourage that and support him and build on that, whatever the obstacles are and however difficult it is.”

Owen recalled that, when David and Ed Miliband were competing for the Labour Party leadership in 2010, she asked MP Jeremy Corbyn who should be the party leader.

“You know what he said? Their mother.”

When asked if Kozak would be among the people risking arrest outside the Labour party conference, Owen responded: “Absolutely, she’d be with us holding a sign.”
